title: Semi-Empirical Mass Formula (Weizsäcker's Formula)
short_intro: The semi-empirical mass formula is a mathematical expression used to predict the binding energy and mass of an atomic nucleus based on the liquid drop model. It accounts for five distinct energetic contributions: volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, and pairing energies.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the individual terms (volume, surface, Coulomb, asymmetry, pairing) of the mass formula, dependence of binding energy on mass number A and atomic number Z, and identifying stable isobars.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed derivation of the volume and surface energy terms, finding the most stable charge Z for a given mass number A by minimization of mass, and calculating beta decay endpoints.

prerequisites: Liquid drop model of the nucleus
Nuclear binding energy and mass defect

concept_notes.heading: Volume Energy Term
bullets: Arises from the short-range attractive nature of strong nuclear forces exhibiting saturation.
Proportional to the total number of nucleons, hence directly proportional to mass number A.
Contributes positively to the total binding energy of the nucleus: E_v = a_v A.

concept_notes.heading: Surface Energy Term
bullets: Correction to the volume term because nucleons on the surface have fewer neighboring nucleons to interact with.
Proportional to the surface area of the nucleus, which scales as R^2 or A^{2/3}.
Acts to decrease the total binding energy: E_s = -a_s A^{2/3}.

concept_notes.heading: Coulomb Energy Term
bullets: Represents the mutual electrostatic repulsion among the Z protons distributed uniformly throughout the nuclear volume.
Proportional to Z(Z-1) and inversely proportional to the nuclear radius R (proportional to A^{1/3}).

concept_notes.heading: Asymmetry and Pairing Energy Terms
bullets: Asymmetry energy accounts for the stability preference of having an equal number of neutrons and protons (N = Z), reducing binding for Z != N.
Pairing energy reflects the quantum mechanical tendency of nucleons to form pairs, making even-even nuclei most stable and odd-odd nuclei least stable.
Asymmetry term: E_a = -a_a \frac{(N-Z)^2}{A}; Pairing term: E_p = \pm \delta(A) or 0 depending on neutron-proton parity.

derivations.title: Derivation of Volume and Surface Energy Terms
derivations.conditions: Assuming the nucleus behaves like an incompressible liquid drop of radius R = r_0 A^{1/3}.
steps: Assume total nuclear volume V is proportional to mass number A, so V = \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = \frac{4}{3} \pi r_0^3 A.
Since each interior nucleon interacts with a constant number of neighbors, the total binding energy due to these interactions is proportional to A, giving the volume term a_v A.
Nucleons on the surface lack neighbors on the outer side, causing a reduction in binding energy proportional to the surface area 4\pi R^2 \propto A^{2/3}.
derivations.result: Binding energy contribution = a_v A - a_s A^{2/3}

derivations.title: Derivation of the Most Stable Charge Z_0 for a Given Mass Number A
derivations.conditions: For odd-A isobars where pairing energy delta is zero, differentiate the mass or binding energy equation with respect to Z.
steps: Write the total binding energy as B(A, Z) = a_v A - a_s A^{2/3} - a_c \frac{Z^2}{A^{1/3}} - a_a \frac{(A-2Z)^2}{A}.
Set the derivative of binding energy with respect to Z equal to zero to find the maximum binding energy (minimum mass): \frac{\partial B}{\partial Z} = 0.

formula_sheet.name: Semi-Empirical Mass Formula (Total Binding Energy)
formula_sheet.equation_html: B(A, Z) = a_v A - a_s A^{2/3} - a_c \frac{Z^2}{A^{1/3}} - a_a \frac{(A-2Z)^2}{A} \pm \delta(A)
formula_sheet.variables: A = mass number, Z = atomic number, a_v, a_s, a_c, a_a = empirical constants, delta = pairing parameter

formula_sheet.name: Nuclear Mass Formula
formula_sheet.equation_html: M(Z, A) = Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n - \frac{1}{c^2} B(A, Z)
formula_sheet.variables: m_p = \text{mass of proton}, m_n = \text{mass of neutron}, c = \text{speed of light}

formula_sheet.name: Condition for Beta Stability
formula_sheet.variables: Z_0 = \text{most stable atomic number for isobar A}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Binding Energy per Nucleon vs Mass Number A
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A smooth curve rising sharply at low A, peaking around A = 50 to 60 near 8.8 MeV, and slowly declining towards heavy nuclei at large A, with points showing experimental scatter.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the competition between volume term (dominant at low-medium A) and Coulomb/surface terms (dominant at large A).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Directly tested for identifying peak stability region (Fe-56) and explaining nuclear fission and fusion.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Mass Parabola for Isobars (Odd vs Even A)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parabolic curves plotting nuclear mass M versus atomic number Z for a fixed mass number A. Two parallel parabolas for even-even and odd-odd, or a single parabola for odd-A.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows why odd-A isobars have one stable beta-decay endpoint, while even-A isobars can have multiple stable isobars due to pairing energy shifts.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Explains double beta decay and the absence of stable odd-odd nuclei (with rare exceptions like H-2, Li-6, B-10, N-14).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Liquid Drop Analogy Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic comparison of surface tension energy in liquid droplets versus nuclear surface energy scaling as A^{2/3}.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Validates the assumption that nuclear forces saturate analogously to intermolecular forces in liquid droplets.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on liquid drop model parameters.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the volume energy contribution to the total binding energy of a nucleus with mass number A = 64, given the volume energy coefficient a_v = 15.8 MeV.
solution_steps: Identify the formula for volume energy: E_v = a_v A.
Substitute the given values: a_v = 15.8 MeV and A = 64.

solved_numericals.question: Using the semi-empirical mass formula, find the surface energy contribution for a nucleus with A = 125, given the surface energy coefficient a_s = 18 MeV.
solution_steps: Identify the formula for surface energy: E_s = a_s A^{2/3}.

solved_numericals.question: For an isobar with mass number A = 27, calculate the asymmetry energy term if the atomic number Z = 13 and asymmetry coefficient a_a = 23 MeV.
solution_steps: Determine the number of neutrons N = A - Z = 27 - 13 = 14.
Identify the asymmetry energy formula: E_a = a_a \frac{(N-Z)^2}{A}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Nucleus is spherical and incompressible with uniform density, limiting applicability to deformed or halo nuclei.
Limitation: Fails for very light nuclei (A < 15) where shell effects and quantum granularity dominate over macroscopic liquid drop behavior.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Coulomb term adds to the nuclear binding energy because protons attract each other.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Coulomb term subtracts from the binding energy.
common_misconceptions.why: Protons experience electrostatic repulsion, which destabilizes the nucleus and reduces total binding energy.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Odd-odd nuclei are the most stable because they have equal numbers of unpaired nucleons.
common_misconceptions.correct: Even-even nuclei are the most stable.
common_misconceptions.why: Nucleon pairing leads to an energetic bonus (pairing energy), making even-even configurations tightly bound and odd-odd the least bound.

quick_revision: Volume term scales as A, surface term as A^{2/3}, Coulomb term as Z^2 A^{-1/3}, asymmetry term as (N-Z)^2 A^{-1}, and pairing term is plus/minus delta for even-even/odd-odd nuclei.
Semi-Empirical Mass Formula (Total Binding Energy): B(A, Z) = a_v A - a_s A^{2/3} - a_c \frac{Z^2}{A^{1/3}} - a_a \frac{(A-2Z)^2}{A} \pm \delta(A)
Volume Energy Term: E_v = a_v A
